newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian party defies military, opens new HQ.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian party defies military, opens new HQ.

text.p: Supporters of Indonesian opposition figurehead Megawati Sukarnoputri opened a new party headquarters on Monday despite the military saying the move was unacceptable.

Megawati, daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted from the leadership of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) in June and was not present at the inauguration of what her followers called the new PDI headquarters, a two-storey building in an eastern Jakarta suburb.
Her supporters said they had told the relevant authorities about the move.

"We have sent letters to the head of the police, to the ABRI (military) chief, to the ministry of home affairs and to police in the area," said Kwik Kian Gie, a close associate of Megawati. "Until today, there has been no reaction."

Republika newspaper quoted Lieutenant-General Syarwan Hamid, chief of the military's social and political affairs division, as saying Megawati's followers do not have the right to carry out political activities. He also said the plan to open the headquarters was unacceptable.
Indonesia's military is allowed by the constitution to have a major say in internal affairs, including politics.
Police are in control of the PDI's main party office in central Jakarta, which they raided on July 27 to evict Megawati's supporters who had taken over the building.
The supporters took over the building after Megawati was ousted from the PDI leadership by a government-backed party faction and replaced by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi.

Analysts have said the government is worried by Megawati's vote-gathering potential in general elections next year, and the possibility she might run against President Suharto in the 1998 presidential poll.
Suharto, who replaced Sukarno in the mid-1960s, has been elected six times unopposed.
"Basically the government only recognises Surjadi as chief of the central executive board of the PDI," Republika quoted Hamid as saying.
The police raid on the party headquarters in July led to the worst riots in Jakarta for more than two decades.
State-owned Antara news agency quoted Attorney-General Singgih as saying on Monday that 123 people had been arrested in connection with the riots, of whom 117 were still in custody.
Singgih, who spoke to reporters after meeting Suharto, said the president wanted them speedily dealt with under the law.
